<p style="font-size:10.0pt;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Indicate by check mark
whether the registrant is a shell company (as defined in Rule&nbsp;12b-2 of the
Exchange Act). Yes </font><font face="Wingdings">o</font> No <font face="Wingdings">&#253;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">At June&nbsp;30, 2005,
the last business day of registrant&#146;s most recently completed second fiscal
quarter, the aggregate market value of shares of common stock held by
non-affiliates of registrant (1)&nbsp;(including fiduciary accounts administered
by affiliates) was $4,091,276,550 based on the last sale price on the Nasdaq
National Market on June&nbsp;30, 2005.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">As of March&nbsp;9, 2006,
123,296,036 shares of common stock were outstanding.</font></p>

held by directors, executive officers, and shares held in fiduciary accounts by
the Registrant and subsidiaries of the registrant with discretionary power to
vote or dispose of such shares as of June&nbsp;30, 2005.&nbsp; Exclusion of
shares held by any person should not be construed to indicate that such person
possesses the power, direct or indirect, to direct or cause the direction of
the management or policies of the registrant, or that such person is controlled
by or under common control with the registrant.</font></p>

<br clear="all" style="page-break-before:always;">


<div style="font-family:Times New Roman;">

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><a name="Parti_155402"></a><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">PART&nbsp;I</font></b></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="font-size:10.0pt;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><a name="Item1_Business_155404"></a><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">ITEM 1.</font></u>&#160; <u>BUSINESS </u></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">General</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Mercantile Bankshares
Corporation, with $16.4 billion in assets for the year ended December&nbsp;31,
2005, is a regional multibank holding company with headquarters in Baltimore,
Maryland.&#160; It is comprised of 11 banks
(the &#147;Banks&#148;) and a mortgage banking company.&#160;
Eight banks are headquartered in Maryland, two are in Virginia and one
is in Delaware.&#160; At December&nbsp;31,
2005, Bankshares&#146; largest bank, Mercantile-Safe Deposit and Trust Company (&#147;MSD&amp;T&#148;),
represented approximately 45% of total assets and operated 40 offices in
Maryland, 13 in Virginia, two in Washington, D.C. and one in Pennsylvania.
MSD&amp;T provides nearly all of Bankshares&#146; substantial wealth management
operations and specialized corporate banking services.&#160; Mercantile Bankshares Corporation was
incorporated under the laws of Maryland on May&nbsp;27, 1969.&#160; Mercantile Bankshares Corporation along with
its consolidated subsidiaries is referred to in this report as &#147;Bankshares,&#148; &#147;we&#148;
or &#147;Registrant.&#148;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Washington Expansion and
Affiliate Consolidation</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In 2004, Bankshares initiated a significant reorganization within its
Banking network.&#160; In a move designed to
create banks of sufficient size and depth to compete more effectively today and
in the future, Bankshares combined 11 affiliate banks to create four new
organizations, all with a more prominent Mercantile identity. This
reorganization has enabled Bankshares to operate more effectively and
efficiently in the face of increased competitive and regulatory pressures.&#160; Fewer, larger banks allow better leverage of
our branch network, reduce administrative and operational redundancies and
increase the breadth and depth of expertise within our banks. All banks that
were combined are geographically contiguous, share increasingly common market
dynamics and offer the opportunity to create scale efficiencies.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">To capitalize on the
potential in affluent, fast growing metropolitan Washington, D.C., in 2004
Bankshares consolidated most of its retail and small business, commercial
lending and real estate operations in the Washington region into its affiliate
bank headquartered in Montgomery County, Maryland, and renamed the bank
Mercantile Potomac Bank (&#147;Mercantile Potomac&#148;). In the second quarter of 2005,
Bankshares consolidated Fidelity Bank, its bank subsidiary in western Maryland,
into Farmers&nbsp;&amp; Mechanics Bank (&#147;Farmers&#148;), its subsidiary bank based
in Frederick, Maryland. The consolidation of these banks enables the surviving
bank to serve its local customers with greater scale and expertise. Also, in
the second quarter of 2005, Mercantile Potomac merged into MSD&amp;T, and
continues to do business in the Washington metropolitan region as a division of
MSD&amp;T under the Mercantile Potomac Bank name. This combination enables
Bankshares to provide the capital resources necessary for greater expansion
into the Washington, D.C. and Northern Virginia markets.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On May&nbsp;18, 2005,
Bankshares completed its acquisition of Community Bank of Northern Virginia (&#147;CBNV&#148;),
a bank headquartered in Sterling, Virginia, which was merged into MSD&amp;T and
became part of MSD&amp;T&#146;s Mercantile Potomac Bank.&#160; CBNV operated 14 branch offices in the
Northern Virginia metropolitan market at the time of the acquisition. The
primary reason for the merger with CBNV was to expand Bankshares&#146; distribution
network in Northern Virginia, a higher growth market. The total consideration
paid to CBNV shareholders in connection with the acquisition was $82.9 million
in cash and 3.7 million shares of Bankshares&#146; common stock, which reflects the
adjustment for the three-for-two stock split announced by Bankshares on January
10, 2006.&#160; CBNV transactions have been
included in Bankshares&#146; financial results subsequent to May&nbsp;18, 2005.&#160; The assets and liabilities of CBNV were
recorded on the Consolidated Balance Sheet at their respective fair values. The
fair values have been determined as of May&nbsp;18, 2005 and are subject to
refinement, as further information becomes available. The transaction resulted
in total assets acquired as of May&nbsp;18, 2005 of $888.2 million, including
$671.0 million of loans and leases; liabilities assumed were $842.3 million,
including $626.9 million of deposits.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Affiliate Bank Network</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Bankshares places
particular emphasis on long-term customer relationships by providing
value-added services through its extensive affiliate bank network.&#160; Each of its affiliate Banks has its own
identity, management team and board of directors.&#160; Perhaps most importantly, each Bank has
strong historical ties to the families and businesses in the community it
serves.&#160; Through its association with
Bankshares, each Bank is able to provide its customers with the sophisticated
banking services and financial resources of a major banking organization.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">1</font></p>

<br clear="all" style="page-break-before:always;">


<div style="font-family:Times New Roman;">

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">For purposes of segment
reporting, two operating components have been identified: Banking and
Investment&nbsp;&amp; Wealth Management. For segment reporting information, see
Note No.&nbsp;16 (Segment Reporting) to the financial statements in Item 8 of
this Annual Report and information under the heading &#147;Segment Reporting&#148; in the
sections captioned &#147;Analysis of Operating Results for 2005 to 2004&#148; and &#147;Review
of Earnings and Balance Sheet for 2004 to 2003,&#148; in Item 7 of this Annual
Report. Bankshares periodically reviews and considers possible acquisitions of
banks and other entities performing related activities and discusses such
possible acquisitions with management of the subject companies, and such
acquisitions, which may be material, may be made from time to time.&#160; Acquisitions are normally subject to
regulatory approval.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Banking Services</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Retail
Banking</font></i></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Banks offer numerous
services to meet the checking, savings, investment and credit needs of
individuals in their communities.&#160; Retail
banking services include checking, savings and money market accounts,
Individual Retirement Accounts, and time deposits.&#160;&#160;&#160; The Banks offer home equity loans and lines
of credit,&#160; installment loans and lines
of credit, and equipment and transportation (auto, marine, recreational
vehicles, aircraft) loans to meet a variety of borrowing needs.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="font-size:10.0pt;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Through the affiliate
bank network, customers have no-fee access to their accounts at 250 Mercantile BANKING TWENTY-FOUR</font><font size="1" style="font-size:7.0pt;position:relative;top:-3.0pt;">SM</font>&#160;ATMs, and they
can perform many routine transactions at any of the 240 affiliate-banking offices.&#160; For added convenience, substantially all of
Bankshares affiliates provide customers with toll-free telephone access to a
centralized Customer Service Center and a voice-response account information
system.&#160; BANKING
TWENTY-FOUR ONLINE<font size="1" style="font-size:7.0pt;position:relative;top:-3.0pt;">&#174;</font>&#160;enables customers to access their personal
accounts online to pay bills, verify account balances, track recent account
activity and perform selected transactions.&nbsp;BANKING&nbsp;TWENTY-FOUR ONLINE offers sole proprietors
similar capabilities specifically tailored to meet small business needs.</p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Small
Business Banking</font></i></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Banks offer numerous
services to meet the deposit, credit and service needs of businesses with
annual<b><font style="font-weight:bold;"> </font></b>revenues up to $3.0 million or credit
needs up to $750.0 thousand. Each Bank works closely with customers to provide
cash management services and extend credit for such purposes as receivables and
inventory financing, equipment leases and real estate financing.<b><i><font style="font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;"> </font></i></b>Where appropriate, the Banks are
adept at employing government guarantee programs, such as those available from
the Small Business Administration.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Commercial
Banking</font></i></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Commercial banking
services include commercial deposit, lending and commercial real estate
solutions provided to businesses with annual revenues between $4.0 million and
$50.0 million.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Cash management services
help business customers collect, transfer and invest their cash.&#160; Through a variety of electronic payment and
account management tools, customers are able to monitor and manage cash flows
conveniently and efficiently.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">With their local knowledge
and focus, our Banks are well suited to meet the traditional credit needs of
businesses in their market areas.&#160; Each
Bank works closely with customers to extend credit for general business
purposes, such as working capital, plant expansion or equipment purchases, and
for financing industrial and commercial real estate.&#160; When local commercial customers do not
qualify for traditional financing, we can help them convert the value of their
accounts receivable, inventory and equipment into cash for operations.
Additionally, we can arrange more sophisticated financing in the areas of
acquisitions and management buyouts. We provide land acquisition and
development, construction and interim financing to commercial real estate
investors and developers.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In addition to extending credit
to the businesses in its own market area, MSD&amp;T works in collaboration with
other affiliates when their customers&#146; credit needs exceed the affiliate bank&#146;s
lending limit or when there is a more specialized commercial banking need. To
supplement traditional credit products, the Banks offer capital market products
such as municipal bond underwriting, interest rate risk management and
financial advisory services through the MSD&amp;T Capital Markets Group. These
services include underwriting and remarketing tax-exempt and taxable municipal
variable-rate demand bonds for nonprofit organizations such as senior living
and health care providers, private schools, health and social welfare
organizations and cultural institutions. By working directly with borrowers, we
can evaluate and recommend financing and interest rate risk management
strategies, which include interest rate swaps, caps and collars.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">3</font></p>

<div>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Mortgage
Banking</font></i></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Residential mortgages are
provided through Mercantile Mortgage, LLC, a joint venture between Mercantile
Mortgage Corporation (&#147;Mercantile Mortgage&#148;), a subsidiary of MSD&amp;T, and
Wells Fargo Ventures, LLC.&#160; A wide
variety of competitively priced fixed- and variable-rate products are
available, including jumbo loans.&#160;
Residential mortgage loans also are available through the Banks.
Mercantile Mortgage also makes loans for land acquisition, development and
construction of single-family and multifamily housing.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Risks associated with residential
mortgage lending include interest rate risk, which is mitigated through the
sale of the majority of all conforming fixed-rate loans, and default risk by
the borrower, which is mitigated through underwriting procedures and credit
quality standards, among other things.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Permanent financing for
multifamily projects and long-term, nonrecourse financing for commercial real
estate are provided through Columbia National Real Estate Finance, LLC (&#147;CNREF&#148;),
a joint venture, the majority of which is owned by Mercantile Mortgage.&#160; CNREF is a Freddie Mac Program Plus Seller
Servicer and is a MAP (Multifamily Accelerated Processing) approved lender for
HUD.&#160; It has correspondent relationships
with approximately 12 life insurance companies and services a loan portfolio in
excess of $6.1 billion. Permanent financing for multifamily projects nationwide
is also provided through HarborPoint Capital, LP, a joint venture, the majority
of which is owned by Mercantile Mortgage.&#160;
HarborPoint Capital, LP, headquartered in Dallas, Texas, is one of the
nation&#146;s few Fannie Mae DUS (Delegated Underwriting and Servicing) lenders.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Insurance Products</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Keller Stonebraker
Insurance,&nbsp;Inc., an independent, wholly owned subsidiary of Farmers&nbsp;&amp;
Mechanics Bank, arranges a full line of consumer insurance products through
offices in Hagerstown and Cumberland, Maryland, and Keyser, West Virginia.&#160; Consumer insurance products include
annuities, homeowners, automobile, life and personal umbrellas.&#160; MBC Agency,&nbsp;Inc. provides as agent,
under group policies, credit life insurance in connection with extensions of
credit by the Banks.&#160; Mercantile Life
Insurance Company reinsures the insurance provided by MBC Agency,&nbsp;Inc.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Potomac Basin Group
Associates,&nbsp;Inc. operates as an independent, wholly owned subsidiary of
Farmers&nbsp;&amp; Mechanics Bank and is an independent insurance agency
specializing in corporate employee benefit plans through its offices in
Beltsville and Ellicott City, Maryland. Keller Stonebraker provides commercial
products that include property and casualty packages, workers&#146; compensation,
professional liability and umbrella coverage, bonds and 401(k) and other
benefit plans.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Investment and Wealth Management
Services</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Bankshares offers
investment and wealth management services through the Investment&nbsp;&amp;
Wealth Management division (&#147;IWM&#148;) of MSD&amp;T.&#160; IWM continues to build on a more than 140-year
tradition of providing investment and wealth management services to private
individuals, family groups and institutions.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Today, Bankshares
provides a range of wealth management services.&#160;
Over the past several years, IWM has developed risk management and asset
allocation analyses to complement the investment advice we offer.&#160; An open architecture platform enables
Bankshares to offer an array of proprietary investment products and carefully
selected outside managers in a range of asset classes, including equity,
fixed-income and alternative investment products.&#160; Bankshares&#146; investment platform provides a
range of investment vehicles, from separate account management to mutual
funds.&#160; Investment and wealth management
services are available through professional advisors at MSD&amp;T, through the
affiliate bank network and through Baltimore-based Mercantile Brokerage Services,&nbsp;Inc.
(&#147;MBSI&#148;).&#160; Asset allocation and risk
management capabilities, coupled with a range of proprietary and nonproprietary
investment alternatives and investment vehicles, enable Bankshares to provide
high quality, advice-driven, risk-managed solutions to meet clients&#146; investment
objectives.&#160; At December&nbsp;31, 2005,
Bankshares had $20.6 billion of discretionary assets under management and $46.5
billion in assets under administration.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Retail
Brokerage Services</font></i></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On November&nbsp;12,
2004, Mercantile consolidated its brokerage activities by merging Mercantile
Securities,&nbsp;Inc., into Peremel&nbsp;&amp; Company,&nbsp;Inc.&#160; The resulting entity is Mercantile Brokerage
Services,&nbsp;Inc., a general securities broker-dealer that offers
full-service, discount and online brokerage capabilities and account services.
Our customers can choose from investments in stocks, bonds, proprietary and
nonproprietary mutual funds, and fixed or variable annuities.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<br clear="all" style="page-break-before:always;">


<div>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Private
Wealth Management Services</font></i></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">When managing a client&#146;s
assets as part of an investment management or trustee relationship, Bankshares
focuses on consistent investment performance and an asset allocation that is
individually designed to meet each client&#146;s risk/return parameters and
investment objectives.&#160; Professional
advisors, working in partnership with our clients, provide access to
proprietary and third-party separate account management, the family of
Mercantile Funds, nonproprietary mutual funds and a variety of alternative
investments.&#160; In addition, IWM provides a
wide range of sophisticated fiduciary and client administrative services,
including trust administration, protection and continuity of trust structures,
estate settlement, estate advice and planning, tax advice and planning and
charitable giving programs. IWM also acts in a custodial capacity for its
clients, providing safekeeping of assets, transaction execution, income
collection, preparation of tax returns and recordkeeping. IWM also specializes
in services designed to meet the unique needs of families with substantial
wealth. We provide a full range of services required to manage seamlessly our
client&#146;s complex, multigenerational financial circumstances. We also provide
guidance in more sophisticated investment strategies, incorporating
nontraditional asset classes such as private equity, real estate and hedge fund
investing.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Private
Banking Services</font></i></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Private Banking Group
provides one point of contact for its clients&#146; deposit, investment and credit
needs, ensuring that these services are delivered within an overall asset
management plan.&#160; Private bankers can
coordinate cash flows, arrange investment of short- and long-term funds and
structure credit arrangements to meet short- to long-term needs. In the fourth
quarter of 2005, the Private Banking Group of MSD&amp;T was consolidated into
the Private Banking Group of IWM. This organizational change will provide
private banking customers with Bankshares&#146; full range of financial services.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Institutional
Investment Management</font></i></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Bankshares, through IWM,
the Banks and Boyd Watterson Asset Management, LLC, works to provide businesses
and charitable organizations with investment management and administrative
services for their employee retirement plans, profit sharing plans and
endowments.&#160; Clients include state and
local government entities, unions, charitable organizations and military
institutions.&#160; For example, IWM is
trustee for a group trust that focuses on commercial real estate investments
for Taft-Hartley pension plans. IWM also can help nonprofit organizations, such
as charitable and philanthropic groups, with annual giving and capital
campaigns, pooled income funds, gift annuities and charitable remainder
trusts.&#160; Bankshares offers corporations
401(k) programs tailored to their specific needs.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Mercantile
Funds</font></i></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">We
offer a full spectrum of mutual funds - from equity funds designed to grow clients&#146;
money over time, to taxable and tax-exempt bond funds designed to offer regular
income payments, to money market funds designed to help clients build a cash
reserve. The Mercantile Funds help clients create well-rounded portfolios
around their goals - with the level of risk and potential for return that makes
the most sense for them.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Managed
by Mercantile Capital Advisors,&nbsp;Inc., an affiliate of MSD&amp;T,
Mercantile Funds utilize the same investment foundation that has brought
Mercantile regional prominence: risk management, in-depth fundamental research
and a product line designed to meet clients&#146; needs.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Private Equity</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Bankshares, in
partnership with MSD&amp;T, began a focused private equity investment
initiative in 2000 with two objectives: provide an alternative method of
funding to develop additional long-term client relationships with emerging
companies in Bankshares&#146; market area and provide an alternative use of capital
to generate long-term returns.&#160; The
primary investments are private equity limited partnerships located, or seeking
investment opportunities, within Bankshares&#146; geographic trade area and, to a
lesser extent, direct investments in privately held companies within the
region. The private equity funds include small- and middle-market buyout funds,
mezzanine funds and late-stage venture funds in which the target investments of
the funds are or have the potential to become Bankshares customers.&#160; For more information on private equity
investments, see Notes No.&nbsp;1, 6 and 10 of the financial statements.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">5</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Employees</font></b></p>

<p align="left" style="line-height:normal;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">At December&nbsp;31, 2005, Bankshares and its
affiliates had approximately 3,606 employees.</font></p>

<p align="left" style="line-height:normal;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<h4 style="font-weight:bold;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;page-break-after:auto;text-autospace:none;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Competition</font></b></h4>

<h4 style="font-weight:bold;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;page-break-after:auto;text-autospace:none;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></b></h4>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">The
banking business is highly competitive. &#160;Within
their service areas, the Banks compete with commercial banks (including local
banks and branches or affiliates of other larger banks), savings and loan
associations and credit unions for loans and deposits, and with insurance
companies and other financial institutions for various types of loans. &#160;There is also competition for commercial and
retail banking business from banks and financial institutions located outside
our service areas. &#160;Interstate banking is
an established part of the competitive environment. &#160;Bankshares is a financial holding company and
is the largest independent bank holding company headquartered in Maryland.&#160; Measured in terms of assets under management
and administration, MSD&amp;T believes it is one of the largest trust
institutions in the mid-Atlantic region of the United States. &#160;MSD&amp;T and its subsidiaries (i.e., Boyd
Watterson&nbsp;&amp; Mercantile Capital Advisors,&nbsp;Inc.) compete for
various classes of fiduciary and investment advisory business with other banks
and trust companies, insurance companies, investment counseling firms, mutual
funds and others. &#160;Mercantile Mortgage is
one of many competitors in its area of activity.&#160; MBC Agency,&nbsp;Inc. is limited to providing
life, health and accident insurance in connection with credit extended by the
Banks.</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">The
Banks ranged in asset size from approximately $178.7 million to $7.2 billion,
at December&nbsp;31, 2005. &#160;They face
competition in their own local service areas as well as from the larger
competitors mentioned above.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">6</font></p>

<br clear="all" style="page-break-before:always;">


<div style="font-family:Times New Roman;">

<p align="center" style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<h4 style="font-weight:bold;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;page-break-after:auto;text-autospace:none;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Supervision and Regulation</font></b></h4>

<h4 style="font-weight:bold;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;page-break-after:auto;text-autospace:none;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></b></h4>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><i><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Bankshares</font></i></b></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">Bankshares,
as a registered bank holding company, is subject to regulation and examination
by the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (the &#147;Federal Reserve
Board&#148;) under the Bank Holding Company Act of 1956, as amended (the &#147;BHC Act&#148;)
and is required to file with the Federal Reserve Board quarterly and annual
reports and such additional information as the Federal Reserve Board may
require pursuant to the BHC Act.&#160; Among
other provisions, the BHC Act and regulations promulgated thereunder require
prior approval of the Federal Reserve Board of the acquisition by Bankshares of
more than 5% of any class of the voting shares of any bank holding company,
bank, or savings association.</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="font-size:10.0pt;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Capital Adequacy</font></i>.&#160; The Banks include seven banks chartered by
the state of Maryland (two of which are members of the Federal Reserve System),
a Delaware-chartered bank, and three national banks (additional information
about the chartering of the Banks is contained in <i><font style="font-style:italic;">The Banks</font></i>,
below).&#160; The Federal Reserve Board,
regulator of bank holding companies and state-chartered banks that are members
of the Federal Reserve System, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (the
&#147;OCC&#148;), the federal regulator of national banks, and the Federal Deposit
Insurance Corporation (the &#147;FDIC&#148;), federal regulator of state-chartered banks
that are not members of the Federal Reserve System and insurer of the deposits
of all U.S. commercial banks, have issued substantially similar risk-based and
leverage capital guidelines applicable to United States banking
organizations.&#160; In addition, these
regulatory agencies may from time to time require that a banking organization maintain
capital above the minimum levels, whether because of its financial condition or
actual or anticipated growth.</p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">The
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation Improvement Act of 1991 (&#147;FDICIA&#148;), among
other things, identifies five capital categories for insured depository
institutions (well capitalized, adequately capitalized, undercapitalized,
significantly undercapitalized and critically undercapitalized) and requires
the respective federal regulatory agencies to implement systems for &#147;prompt
corrective action&#148; for insured depository institutions that do not meet minimum
capital requirements within such categories. &#160;FDICIA imposes progressively more restrictive
constraints on operations, management and capital distributions, depending on
the category in which an institution is classified. &#160;Failure to meet the capital guidelines could
also subject a banking institution to requirements to raise capital.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">The
various regulatory agencies have adopted substantially similar regulations that
define the five capital categories identified by FDICIA, using the total
risk-based capital, Tier 1 risk-based capital and leverage capital ratios as
the relevant capital measures. &#160;Such
regulations establish various degrees of corrective action to be taken when an
institution is considered undercapitalized. &#160;Under the regulations, a &#147;well capitalized&#148;
institution must have a Tier 1 risk-based capital ratio of at least six
percent, a total risk-based capital ratio of at least ten percent and a
leverage ratio of at least five percent and not be subject to a capital directive
order.&#160; As of December&nbsp;31, 2005, the
most recent notification from the primary regulators for each of Bankshares&#146;
subsidiary banks categorized them as &#147;well capitalized&#148; under the prompt
corrective action regulations. </font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Changes to the risk-based capital regime for banking organizations are
proposed or implemented from time to time. The minimum risk-based capital
requirements that are currently in effect for U.S. banking organizations follow
the Capital Accord issued in 1988 by the Basel Committee on Banking
Supervision, which is comprised of bank supervisors and central banks from the
major industrialized countries, including the United States.&#160; The Basel Committee issued a proposed
replacement for the 1988 Capital Accord in 2001 (&#147;Basel II&#148;), and work has
continued on the details of Basel II and the timing of its implementation since
that time.&#160; What form any changes to the
risk-based capital requirements may take, the extent of their applicability to
a bank holding company such as Bankshares, and the impact they might have on
Bankshares and its subsidiaries cannot be determined at this time.&#160; Additional information regarding capital
requirements for bank Additional information regarding capital requirements for
bank holding companies and tables reflecting Bankshares&#146; regulatory capital
position at December&nbsp;31, 2005 can be found in Note No.&nbsp;11 (Shareholders&#146;
Equity) to the financial statements in Item 8 of this Annual Report.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">7</font></p>

<br clear="all" style="page-break-before:always;">


<div style="font-family:Times New Roman;">

<p align="center" style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;font-size:10.0pt;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><i><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">The
Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act</font></i><font color="black" style="color:windowtext;">.&#160; The
Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act of 1999 (the &#147;GLB Act&#148;) was adopted on November&nbsp;12,
1999 and amended several of the federal banking laws, including the BHC Act and
the Banking Act of 1933 (generally known as &#147;Glass-Steagall&#148;), that affect
Bankshares and its subsidiaries.&#160; Prior
to the adoption of the GLB Act, the activities of bank holding companies and
their subsidiaries were restricted to banking, the business of managing and
controlling banks, and other activities that the Federal Reserve Board had determined
were so closely related to banking or managing or controlling banks as to be a
proper incident thereto.&#160; In particular,
Glass-Steagall and the BHC Act imposed important restrictions on the ability of
bank holding companies or their subsidiaries to engage in the securities or
insurance business.</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">The GLB
Act repealed the provisions of Glass-Steagall and restrictions in the BHC Act
that limited affiliations among, and overlapping business activities between
the banking business and, respectively, the securities and insurance
industries.&#160; With the adoption of the GLB
Act, a bank holding company that makes an effective election to become a &#147;financial
holding company&#148; may, within a holding company system, (a)&nbsp;engage in
banking, or managing or controlling banks; (b)&nbsp;perform certain servicing
activities for subsidiaries; and (c)&nbsp;engage in any activity, or acquire
and retain the shares of any company engaged in any activity that is either (i)&nbsp;financial
in nature or incidental to such financial activity, as determined by the
Federal Reserve Board in consultation with the Secretary of the Treasury or (ii)&nbsp;complementary
to a financial activity and that does not pose a substantial risk to the safety
and soundness of depository institutions or the financial system generally, as
determined by the Federal Reserve Board.&#160;
Activities that are &#147;financial in nature&#148; include activities specified
in the GLB Act and those activities that the Federal Reserve Board had
determined, by order or regulation in effect prior to enactment of the GLB Act,
to be so closely related to banking or managing or controlling banks as to be a
proper incident thereto.&#160; Thus, a
financial holding company may engage in a full range of banking, securities and
insurance activities, including securities and insurance underwriting, as well
as, subject to certain restrictions, merchant banking activities.&#160; The election to become a financial holding
company is only available to bank holding companies whose bank and thrift
subsidiaries are well capitalized, well managed, and have satisfactory
Community Reinvestment Act ratings.</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">With
exceptions for insurance underwriting, merchant banking and real estate
investment and development, the GLB Act also permits comparable expansion of
national bank activities by banks meeting similar criteria, together with
certain additional firewalls and other requirements, through &#147;financial
subsidiaries&#148; of national banks.&#160;
Similarly, as a matter of Federal law, but still subject to State law,
the GLB Act expands the potential financial activities of subsidiaries of State
banks.&#160; Bankshares filed an election and,
on December&nbsp;20, 2002, became a financial holding company.</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">The GLB
Act also imposed a general scheme of functional regulation with respect to the
activities of bank holding companies and their bank and nonbank subsidiaries to
ensure that banking activities are regulated by bank regulators, securities
activities are regulated by securities regulators, and insurance activities are
regulated by insurance regulators, although the Federal Reserve Board retains
its role as the umbrella supervisor for bank holding companies.&#160; Consequently, various securities activities
of bank subsidiaries of Bankshares are now subject to regulation by the
Securities and Exchange Commission and the National Association of Securities
Dealers,&nbsp;Inc.&#160; The functional
regulation of the securities brokerage activities of banks is not yet fully
implemented.</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">As a
result of the functional regulation imposed by the GLB Act, the Banks have
moved certain securities activities that have become subject to Securities and
Exchange Commission regulation into separate securities subsidiaries or
affiliates.&#160; For example, MSD&amp;T has
two subsidiaries that engage in securities activities:&#160; Mercantile Capital Advisors,&nbsp;Inc., a
registered investment adviser that advises the Mercantile family of mutual
funds and certain other institutional accounts; and Mercantile Brokerage
Services,&nbsp;Inc. (formerly Mercantile Securities,&nbsp;Inc. or Hopkins Plaza
Securities,&nbsp;Inc.), a registered broker-dealer that facilitates the
purchase of shares of mutual funds by bank customers and may engage in certain
other activities in the future.</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">The GLB
Act also implements a number of requirements designed to protect the privacy of
customer information. A financial institution must inform its customers at the
outset of the customer relationship, and at least annually thereafter, of the
institution&#146;s privacy policies and procedures with respect to the customer&#146;s
nonpublic personal financial information.&#160;
With certain exceptions, an institution may not provide any nonpublic
personal information to unaffiliated third parties unless the customer has been
informed that such information may be so provided and the customer has been
given the opportunity to opt out.&#160;
Furthermore, the GLB Act limits a financial institution&#146;s use of a
customer&#146;s account information for marketing purposes and imposes criminal
penalties for the use of fraudulent or deceptive means to obtain personal
customer financial information.&#160; The GLB
Act permits states to adopt more rigorous laws with respect to privacy of
customer information.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">8</font></p>

<br clear="all" style="page-break-before:always;">


<div style="font-family:Times New Roman;">

<p align="center" style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;font-size:10.0pt;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><i><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">The Fair
Credit Reporting Act and the Fair and Accurate Transactions Act of 2003</font></i><font color="black" style="color:windowtext;">.&#160;
The Fair Credit Reporting Act (&#147;FCRA&#148;), among other provisions,
restricts any bank from sharing with its affiliates certain information
relating to its individual customers&#146; creditworthiness and certain other
matters with various exceptions.&#160; &#160;FCRA preempts state laws that purport to
restrict further such information sharing among affiliated institutions.&#160; The Fair and Accurate Transactions Act of
2003 (the &#147;FACT Act&#148;), which was signed into law on December&nbsp;4, 2003, amended
FCRA in various respects, including to enhance the ability of consumers to
combat identity theft, increase the accuracy of consumer credit reports, and
allow consumers to exercise greater control over the type and amount of
marketing solicitations that they receive.&#160;
The new marketing restrictions, with some exceptions, would prevent
banks from using certain information received from an affiliate for marketing
to a consumer unless the consumer was given notice and an opportunity to opt
out.&#160; The FACT Act also restricts the
sharing of certain types of consumer medical information among affiliates.&#160; These new restrictions on sharing or using
information shared among affiliates must be implemented by regulations, which
were issued for public comment but have not yet been finalized.&#160; More generally, the Federal Reserve Board and
the Federal Trade Commission issued joint final rules&nbsp;establishing December&nbsp;1,
2004 as the effective date for many of the provisions of the FACT.</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In December&nbsp;2004, implementing section&nbsp;216 of the FACT Act,
the federal bank regulatory agencies announced interagency final rules&nbsp;to
require financial institutions to adopt measures for properly disposing of &#147;consumer
information&#148; derived from credit reports.&#160;
Federal banking law requires financial institutions to protect customer
information by implementing information security programs.&#160; The rules&nbsp;adopted by the banking
agencies require institutions to make certain adjustments to their information
security programs to include measures for the proper disposal of consumer
information.&#160; The rules&nbsp;define &#147;consumer
information&#148; to mean &#147;any record about an individual, whether in paper,
electronic, or other form, that is a consumer report or is derived from a
consumer report and that is maintained or otherwise possessed by or on behalf
of the [institution] for a business purpose,&#148; and include a compilation of such
records, but exclude any record that does not identify an individual.&#160; The rules&nbsp;took effect on July&nbsp;1,
2005. &#160;Federal regulators have pursued
enforcement action against U.S. banks and other entities for failing to
properly safeguard customers&#146; information.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;font-size:10.0pt;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><i><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">The USA
PATRIOT ACT</font></i><font color="black" style="color:windowtext;">.&#160; Congress adopted the USA PATRIOT ACT (the &#147;Patriot
Act&#148;) on October&nbsp;26, 2001 in response to the terrorist attacks that
occurred on September&nbsp;11, 2001.&#160;
Under the Patriot Act, banks are required to maintain and prepare
additional records and reports that are designed to assist the government&#146;s
efforts to combat terrorism.&#160; The Patriot
Act includes sweeping anti-money laundering and financial transparency laws and
required additional regulations, including, among other things, standards for
verifying client identification when opening an account and rules&nbsp;to
promote cooperation among financial institutions, regulators and law
enforcement entities in identifying parties that may be involved in terrorism
or money laundering.&#160; Specifically, the
customer identification program (&#147;CIP&#148;) regulation issued under the Patriot Act
requires each bank to implement a written CIP appropriate for its size and type
of business that includes certain minimum requirements. The CIP must be
incorporated into the bank&#146;s anti-money laundering compliance program, which is
subject to approval by the bank&#146;s board of directors.&#160; The regulation applies to all federally
regulated banks and savings associations, credit unions, and non-federally
regulated private banks, trust companies, and credit unions. All banks were
required to comply with the CIP regulation for all accounts established on or
after October&nbsp;1, 2003.</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;font-size:10.0pt;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><i><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Interstate
Banking.&#160; &#160;</font></i><font color="black" style="color:windowtext;">Pursuant to the Riegle-Neal Interstate Banking and
Branching Efficiency Act of 1994 (the &#147;Interstate Banking and Branching Act&#148;),
a bank holding company may acquire banks located in states other than its home
state without regard to the permissibility of such acquisitions under state
law, but subject to any state requirement that the bank has been organized and
operating for a minimum period of time, not to exceed five years, and the
requirement that the bank holding company, after the proposed acquisition,
controls no more than 10%&#160; of the total
amount of deposits of insured depository institutions in the United States and
no more than 30%&#160; or such lesser or
greater amount set by state law of such deposits in that state.</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">Subject
to certain restrictions, the Interstate Banking and Branching Act also
authorizes banks to merge across state lines to create interstate banks. &#160;The Interstate Banking and Branching Act also
permits a bank to open new branches in a state in which it does not already
have banking operations if such state enacts a law permitting de novo
branching.</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="font-size:10.0pt;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Other Regulatory Matters</font></i>. &#160;Bankshares is a separate and distinct legal
entity from its subsidiaries.&#160; It
receives substantially all of its revenue from dividends from its subsidiaries
and interest payments from the Banks on subordinated debt. These dividends are
the principal source of funds to pay dividends on Bankshares&#146; common stock and
interest on its debt. The payment of dividends by a bank is subject to federal
law restrictions as well as to the laws of its state of incorporation in the
case of a state-chartered bank. Also, a parent company&#146;s right to participate
in a distribution of assets upon a subsidiary&#146;s</p>

<p align="center" style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">9</font></p>

<p align="center" style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">liquidation or reorganization is subject to the prior claims of the
subsidiary&#146;s creditors.&#160; It is Federal
Reserve Board policy that a bank holding company should serve as a source of
financial and managerial strength for, and commit resources to support each, of
its subsidiary banks even in circumstances in which it might not do so (or may
not legally be required or financially able to do so) absent such a policy.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Changes in control of Bankshares and the Banks are regulated under the
BHC Act, the Change in Bank Control Act of 1978 and various state laws.</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">&#160;In addition to the specific laws and
regulations discussed above, there are numerous federal and state laws and
regulations which regulate the activities of Bankshares and the Banks,
including requirements and limitations relating to reserves, permissible
investments and lines of business, transactions with officers, directors and
affiliates, loan limits, consumer protection laws, privacy of financial
information, predatory lending, fair lending, mergers and acquisitions,
issuances of securities, dividend payments, inter-affiliate liabilities,
extensions of credit and branch banking.&#160;
The BHC Act and the Federal Reserve Board&#146;s regulations limit the
ability of bank subsidiaries of bank holding companies to engage in certain
tie-in arrangements with bank holding companies and their nonbank subsidiaries
in connection with any extension of credit or provision of any property or
services, subject to various exceptions.</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">The laws
and regulations to which Bankshares is subject are constantly under review by
Congress, regulatory agencies and state legislatures.&#160; The likelihood and timing of any bank-related
proposals or legislation and the impact they might have on Bankshares and its
subsidiaries cannot be determined at this time.</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">As a general matter, the recent regulatory environment for banking
organizations has included significant enforcement actions by banking
regulators and other federal and state agencies, involving such matters as
alleged shortcomings in anti-money laundering policies and procedures,
inadequate protection of confidential customer information, and violations of
securities or other laws.&#160; As a result of
this regulatory environment, banking organizations may experience increases in
compliance requirements and associated costs.</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><i><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">The Banks</font></i></b></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">All the
Banks, with the exception of The Citizens National Bank, The National Bank of
Fredericksburg, Marshall National Bank and Trust Company and Mercantile
Peninsula Bank are Maryland banks, subject to the banking laws of Maryland and
to regulations issued by the Commissioner of Financial Regulation of Maryland,
who is required by statute to make at least one examination in each calendar
year (or at 18-month intervals if the Commissioner determines that an
examination is unnecessary in a particular calendar year).&#160; Their deposits are insured by, and they are
subject to certain provisions of federal law and regulations and examination
by, the FDIC.</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">In
addition, The Annapolis Banking and Trust Company and Farmers&nbsp;&amp;
Mechanics Bank are members of the Federal Reserve System and are thereby
subject to regulation by the Federal Reserve Board.</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">The
Citizens National Bank, The National Bank of Fredericksburg and Marshall

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">Mercantile

to regulation by the Delaware State Bank Commissioner, who is required by

Its deposits are insured by, and it is subject to certain provisions of

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Bankshares and its
affiliates are subject to the provisions of Section&nbsp;23A and Section&nbsp;23B
of the Federal Reserve Act and the Federal Reserve Board&#146;s Regulation W, which
implements Sections 23A and 23B.&#160; Section&nbsp;23A,
among other things, limits the amount of loans or extensions of credit by the
Banks to, and their investments in, Bankshares and the nonbank affiliates of
the Banks, while Section&nbsp;23B generally requires that transactions between
the Banks and Bankshares and its nonbank affiliates be on terms and under<b><font style="font-weight:bold;"> </font></b>circumstances that are substantially the same as with
non-affiliates.&#160; Under the
cross-guarantee provisions of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act, in the event
of a loss suffered or anticipated by the FDIC either as a result of default of
a bank subsidiary or related to FDIC assistance provided to a bank subsidiary
in danger of default&nbsp;the Banks may be assessed for the FDIC&#146;s loss,
subject to certain exceptions.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><i><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Other Affiliates</font></i></b></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">As
affiliates of Bankshares, the nonbank affiliates are subject to examination by
the Federal Reserve Board and, as affiliates of the Banks, they are subject to
examination by the FDIC, the Commissioner of Financial Regulation of Maryland
and the OCC, as the case may be.&#160; In
addition, MBC Agency,&nbsp;Inc. and Mercantile Life Insurance Company are subject
to licensing and regulation by state insurance authorities.&#160; Mercantile Capital Advisors,&nbsp;Inc., Boyd
Watterson and Mercantile Brokerage Services,&nbsp;Inc. are subject to
regulation by the Securities and Exchange Commission and state securities law
authorities, and Mercantile Brokerage Services,&nbsp;Inc. is also subject to
regulation by the National Association of Securities Dealers,&nbsp;Inc.&#160; Retail sales of insurance and securities
products by Mercantile Brokerage Services,&nbsp;Inc. are also subject to the
requirements of the Interagency Statement on Retail Sales of Nondeposit
Investment Products promulgated in 1994 by the FDIC, the Federal Reserve Board,
the Comptroller of the Currency and the Office of Thrift Supervision.</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><i><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Effects of Monetary Policy</font></i></b></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">All
commercial banking operations are affected by the Federal Reserve System&#146;s
conduct of monetary policy and its policies change from time to time based on
changing circumstances.&#160; The Federal
Reserve Board effectively controls the supply of bank credit in order to achieve
economic results it deems appropriate, including efforts to combat
unemployment, recession or inflationary pressures.&#160; Among the instruments of monetary policy used
to advance these objectives are open market operations in the purchase and sale
of U.S. Government securities, changes in the discount rate charged on bank
borrowings and changes in reserve requirements against bank deposits.&#160; These means are used in varying combinations
to influence the general level of interest rates and the general availability
of credit.&#160; More specifically, actions by
the Federal Reserve Board influence the levels of interest rates paid on
deposits and other bank funding sources and charged on bank loans as well as
the availability of bank funds with which loans and investments can be made.</font></p>

<p style="color:blue;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" color="black" face="Times New Roman" style="color:windowtext;font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
