<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Allowance for Loan Losses</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The allowance for loan losses is comprised of specific allocations to
impaired loans, general allocations to pools of loans not deemed impaired and
an unallocated amount.&#160; Current trends
and economic conditions that affect the collectibility of the loan portfolio
are incorporated into the general allocation.&#160;
These can include, but are not limited to, exposure to an industry
experiencing problems, changes in the nature or volume of the portfolio,
delinquency and nonaccrual trends.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The specific allowance allocation is based on an analysis of the loan
portfolio by each affiliate bank and Loan Review.&#160; Each loan with an outstanding balance in
excess of a specified threshold that is either on nonaccrual status or on the
Watchlist is evaluated. The Watchlist represents loans identified and closely
followed by management.&#160; They possess
certain qualities or characteristics that may lead to collection and loss
issues.&#160; Monitored loans, which are
included in the Watchlist, display additional risk characteristics suggesting
that they may be classified as nonperforming loans in the near future.&#160; The identified loans are evaluated for
potential loss in accordance with SFAS No.&nbsp;114 and SFAS No.&nbsp;118 by
analyzing current collateral values or present values of cash flows, as well as
the capacity of the guarantor, as applicable.&#160;
The specific allocation resulting from this review decreased 60.4% to
$4.2 million from $10.6 million at December&nbsp;31, 2005 and 2004,
respectively, and was related to specific loan balances of $12.0 million and $18.4
million.&#160; The decrease was largely
attributable to the payoff of a credit exposure at MSD&amp;T during the fourth
quarter of 2005.&#160; Two credit exposures at
MSD&amp;T accounted for $3.5 million, based on the fair value of the
collateral, of the specific allocation at December&nbsp;31, 2005.&#160; See &#147;Nonperforming Assets&#148; in the following section&nbsp;for more
detail.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">41</font></p>

<div style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><hr size="2" width="100%" noshade color="gray" align="left"></div>

</div>
<!-- SEQ.=1,FOLIO='41',FILE='C:\JMS\sethu\06-1934-1\task911748\1934-1-ba-03.htm',USER='sesankaran',CD='Mar 13 22:26 2006' -->


<br clear="all" style="page-break-before:always;">


<div>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The general allowance calculation, which is completed on a quarterly
basis, begins with segmentation of the remaining (unimpaired) portfolio
according to loan types.&#160; Historical loss
factors are maintained for each loan type, providing the starting point of the analysis.
Historical loss factors are applied to all non-Watchlist loans.&#160; Management is currently utilizing the past
five-year loss history specific to each major segment to perform the allocation.&#160; Bankshares also has developed data on
probability of default and loss given default, which have been incorporated for
the higher risk rated credits, which include Watchlist loans that are not
currently impaired.&#160; Those loss factors
are then applied to all loans within the same risk rating.&#160; Qualitative factors that may cause credit
losses to deviate from average historical experience are then developed.&#160; These include, but are not limited to:
changes in the volume and severity of past due loans; changes in the volume of
Watchlist loans and nonaccruals; concentrations in a specific industry or
geographic location; administrative risk concerns that include changes in the
loan review and loan grading system; changes in lending policies and procedures
(which include underwriting, collection, charge-off and recovery practices);
changes in management or the staff of any previously mentioned areas; and
current economic conditions and indicators.&#160;
Both internal and external peer data are utilized as applicable to
establish these factors.&#160; Management&#146;s
judgment and experience are key to this process.&#160; These factors are revised to address current
conditions and trends in the portfolio.&#160;
The general allowance was $133.7 million and $116.7 million at December&nbsp;31,
2005 and 2004, respectively.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The combination of specific and general allowance calculations resulted
in $137.9 million being allocated to loan portfolio segments at December&nbsp;31,
2005 compared with $127.3 million at December&nbsp;31, 2004.&#160; The increase in the allocated allowance is
primarily attributable to the $7.1 million allowance related to the CBNV
acquisition.&#160; The allocation to the
commercial and leasing portfolio has continued to decrease as management has
made significant progress in resolving nonperforming loans in this
segment.&#160; This segment has been the major
beneficiary of the decrease in the specific allowance.&#160; The increased allocations to the commercial
real estate, construction, residential real estate and consumer loan portfolios
are related to the growth in these portfolios, which include balances added as
a result of the CBNV acquisition.&#160; The
decline in the allocation to the home equity lines portfolio is attributable to
improving credit quality metrics.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The allowance amount not allocated represents the differential between
the combined specific and general allocations and the actual allowance.&#160; The unallocated allowance recognizes the
imprecision inherent in estimating and measuring loss when allocating the
allowance to individual, or pools of, loans.&#160;
It is designed to capture fully probable incurred losses in the loan
portfolio after taking into consideration these perspectives.&#160; It takes into consideration the allowance
level deemed appropriate by each affiliate based on its local knowledge and
input from their regulators, including their view from the standpoint of safety
and soundness, among other factors.&#160; The
amount of this component and its relationship to the total allowance for loan
losses may change from one period to another.&#160;
At December&nbsp;31, 2005, the unallocated component of the allowance
for loan losses was $18.8 million, or 12.0%, of the allowance for loan losses.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">During 2005, management engaged a third-party vendor to begin building
a migration model to enhance the allocation methodology of the allowance for
loan losses.&#160; When completed, this model
will replace the in-house model currently utilized by management.&#160; In anticipation of this project, during 2004,
management completed a project to enhance its risk-rating categories to provide
more granularity in assessing the overall risk profile of the loan
portfolio.&#160; Management expects to convert
to the migration model during 2006.&#160; In
addition, the model will evaluate draws against committed, unused lines of
credit and project expected losses related to unused lines of credit.&#160; Any reserve for losses on unfunded lines of
credit must be accounted for as a liability, separate from the allowance for
possible loan losses.&#160; Management does
not expect that this refinement of the credit-risk analysis will have a
material effect on its operating results or its financial position.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The allowance for loan losses has been established through provisions
for loan losses against income.&#160; Loans
deemed uncollectible are charged against the allowance for loan losses and any
subsequent recoveries are credited to the allowance.&#160; The total allowance for loan losses increased
by $7.6 million from year-end 2004 to $156.7 million at December&nbsp;31, 2005,
which reflected the addition of $7.1 million of CBNV&#146;s allowance at
consummation under SOP 03-3, &#147;Accounting for Certain Loans or Debt Securities
Acquired in a Transfer.&#148; The allowance for loan losses as a percent of loans
declined to 1.35% at December&nbsp;31, 2005 compared with 1.46% at December&nbsp;31,
2004.&#160; This reflects overall improving
credit quality trends, the disposition of previously mentioned problem credits
and the inclusion of the acquired portfolio, which resulted in a lower required
allowance as a percentage of loans.&#160;
During 2005, the provision for loan loss expense was $1.6 million
compared with $7.2 million in 2004.&#160; Net
charge-offs decreased to $1.0 million during 2005 compared with $13.6 million
during 2004, mainly due to moderating trends in the level of new nonperforming
assets, our strategic decision to actively manage down problem loans and a
higher level of recoveries during the period.&#160;
The consumer portfolio represented the largest net charge-off amount for
2005 at $1.4 million.&#160; Net charge-offs as
a percent of average loans were 0.01%, 0.14% and 0.11% for the years ended December&nbsp;31,
2005, 2004 and 2003, respectively.&#160;
Intensive collection efforts continue after a loan is charged off in
order to maximize the recovery of amounts previously charged off.&#160; Recoveries as a percent of loans charged off
were 86.9% in 2005, 26.3% in 2004 and 30.4% in 2003.&#160; Recoveries in a given year may not relate to
loans charged off in that year.&#160; Further
details related to the allowance for loan losses are shown in the tables above
and in Note No.&nbsp;4 (Loans and Allowance for Loan Losses) of the financial
statements.</font></p>

<div style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><hr size="1" width="25%" noshade color="black" align="left"></div>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">(1)&nbsp;Aggregate gross interest income of $2.1 million and $2.5
million in 2005 and 2004, respectively, on nonaccrual and renegotiated loans
would have been recorded if these loans had been accruing on their original
terms throughout the period or since origination if held for part of the
period.&#160; The amount of interest income on
the nonaccrual and renegotiated loans that was recorded totaled
$0.5&nbsp;million and $0.8 million in 2005 and 2004, respectively.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Nonperforming Assets</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Nonperforming assets consist of nonaccrual loans, renegotiated loans
and other real estate owned (i.e., real estate acquired in foreclosure or in
lieu of foreclosure).&#160; With respect to
nonaccrual loans, our policy is that, regardless of the value of the underlying
collateral and/or guarantees, no interest is accrued on the entire balance once
either principal or interest payments on any loan are 90 days past due at the
end of a calendar quarter.&#160; All accrued
and uncollected interest on such loans is reversed out of interest income and
is recognized only as it is collected.&#160;
If a loan is impaired and has a specific loss allocation based on an
analysis under SFAS No.&nbsp;114, &#147;Accounting by Creditors for Impairment of a
Loan &#150; an amendment of FASB Statements No.&nbsp;5 and 15,&#148; all payments are
applied against the loan&#146;s principal.&#160; A
loan may be placed on nonaccrual status sooner than this standard if, in
management&#146;s judgment, such action is warranted.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Nonperforming assets as a percentage of period-end loans and other real
estate owned were 0.20% at December&nbsp;31, 2005 compared with 0.30% in the
preceding year.&#160; At year-end 2005,
nonperforming assets were $23.2 million compared with $31.1 million at year-end
2004.&#160; Nonperforming loans totaled $22.6
million at December&nbsp;31, 2005 compared with $30.9 million at December&nbsp;31,
2004.&#160; The largest dollar decrease in
nonperforming loans was $9.7 million in the commercial and leasing category,
which accounted for 69.9% of nonperforming loans at December&nbsp;31,
2005.&#160; The decrease in nonperforming
loans was due primarily to improvement in credit quality at the lead bank,
MSD&amp;T.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The level of monitored loans, or loans with characteristics suggesting
that they may be classified as nonperforming in the near future, decreased
during the year.&#160; At December&nbsp;31,
2005, monitored loans were $2.2 million compared with $6.4 million a year
before. Contributing to this decrease was the elimination of the one remaining
loan secured by a commercial aircraft.&#160;
The amount of loans past due 30-89 days increased from $51.5 million at December&nbsp;31,
2004 to $65.2 million at December&nbsp;31, 2005.&#160; This increase was primarily reflected in the
construction loan category and in a general increase in loans past due 30
days.&#160; At the acquisition date,
Bankshares determined that two loans at CBNV were deemed to be impaired and
were subject to SOP 03-3.&#160; These loans
had a $4.9 million contractual balance and a $3.5 million carrying value at December&nbsp;31,
2005 and the estimated cash flows are assessed at each quarter-end.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Other real estate owned was $667 thousand at December&nbsp;31, 2005
compared with $212 thousand at December&nbsp;31, 2004.&#160; These properties generally are sold within a
short period, therefore, regardless of the amount, the properties generally
will have changed from year to year.&#160;
Other real estate owned is carried at the lower of cost or fair market
value.&#160; Refer to the data in the &#147;Nonperforming
Assets&#148; table above, which shows the changes in the amounts of various
categories of nonperforming assets over the last five years and sets forth the
relationship between nonperforming loans and total loans.</font></p>

  <p align="right" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:right;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">8,267,693</font></p>
  </td>
  <td width="0%" valign="bottom" bgcolor="#CCEEFF" style="background:#CCEEFF;padding:0in 0in 0in 0in;width:.9%;">
  <p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:1.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
  </td>

</table>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Of the $5.4 billion in loans maturing after one year, $2.6 billion, or
47.3%, have fixed interest rates, and $2.8 billion, or 52.7%, have variable interest
rates.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Asset/Liability and Market Risk Management</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Asset/liability management involves the evaluation, monitoring and
management of interest rate risk, market risk, liquidity and funding.&#160; The Asset/Liability Management Committee (&#147;ALCO&#148;)
oversees policy guidelines and reports periodically to the Board of
Directors.&#160; This Committee consists of
senior financial and business executives.&#160;
Treasury division management and other finance personnel monitor the
day-to-day exposure to interest rates in response to loan and deposit flows.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Interest Rate Risk</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Interest rate risk, which potentially can have a significant earnings
impact, is an integral part of being a financial intermediary. Bankshares is
subject to interest rate risk due to a variety of factors including:</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="font-size:10.0pt;margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;text-autospace:none;text-indent:-.25in;"><font size="3" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:12.0pt;">&#149;</font><font size="1" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font>Assets and
liabilities may mature or reprice at different times (for example, currently
our assets reprice slightly faster than our liabilities and if interest rates
fall, earnings will initially decline);</p>

<p style="font-size:10.0pt;margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;text-autospace:none;text-indent:-.25in;"><font size="3" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:12.0pt;">&#149;</font><font size="1" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font>Assets and
liabilities may reprice at the same time but by different amounts (for example,
when the market level of interest rates is falling, we may reduce rates paid on
checking and savings deposit accounts by an amount that is less than the
general decline in market interest rates);</p>

<p style="font-size:10.0pt;margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;text-autospace:none;text-indent:-.25in;"><font size="3" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:12.0pt;">&#149;</font><font size="1" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font>Short-term and
long-term market interest rates may change by different amounts (i.e., the
shape of the yield curve may affect new loan and investment yields and funding
costs differently); or</p>

<p style="font-size:10.0pt;margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;text-autospace:none;text-indent:-.25in;"><font size="3" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:12.0pt;">&#149;</font><font size="1" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font>The remaining
maturity of various assets or liabilities may shorten or lengthen as interest
rates change (for example, if long-term mortgage rates fall, mortgage-backed
securities may prepay significantly earlier than anticipated, which could
reduce portfolio income). In addition, interest rate changes have an indirect
impact on loan demand, credit losses, mortgage originations, the value of
mortgage servicing rights and other sources of earnings.</p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;text-autospace:none;text-indent:-.25in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">A balance sheet is considered asset-sensitive when its assets (loans
and securities) reprice faster or to a greater extent than liabilities
(deposits and borrowings).&#160; An
asset-sensitive balance sheet will produce more net interest income when rates
rise and less net interest income when rates fall.&#160; A balance sheet is described as
liability-sensitive when its liabilities (deposits or borrowings) reprice more
frequently or to a greater degree than its assets (loans and securities).&#160; A liability-sensitive balance sheet will
produce a lower level of net interest income when interest rates rise and more
net interest income when rates fall.&#160;
Bankshares&#146; large and relatively rate- insensitive deposit base funds a
portfolio with a large percentage of floating-rate commercial and consumer
loans, which creates a bias towards asset sensitivity.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">To manage this asset sensitivity in our balance sheet, we maintain a
large portfolio of fixed-rate, although short-duration, investments.
Periodically, we elect to use derivatives to protect assets and liabilities
from changes in interest rates.&#160; When
deciding whether to use derivatives instead of cash market instruments to
achieve the same goal, we consider a number of factors, such as cost,
efficiency, the effect on our liquidity and capital, and our overall
strategy.&#160; The derivatives we use for
interest rate risk management purposes are primarily interest rate swaps.&#160; We fully incorporate the market risk
associated with interest rate risk management derivatives into our</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">44</font></p>

<div>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">earnings simulation model in the same manner as other on-balance-sheet
financial instruments.&#160; The credit risk
amount and estimated net fair value of these derivatives as of December&nbsp;31,
2005 and 2004 are presented in Note No.&nbsp;18 (Derivative Instruments and
Hedging Activities) to the financial statements.&#160;&#160; Derivatives are used for asset/liability
management in three ways:&#160; (1)&nbsp;to
convert long-term fixed-rate debt to floating-rate payments by entering into
receive-fixed swaps at issuance; (2)&nbsp;to convert the cash flows from
selected asset and/or liability instruments/portfolios from fixed to floating
payments or vice versa; and (3)&nbsp;to hedge the mortgage origination pipeline
by utilizing forward commitments for loans held-for-sale.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">We assess interest rate risk by comparing projected net interest income
in the current rate environment with various interest rate scenarios that
differ in the direction of interest rate changes, the degree of change over
time, the speed of the change and the projected shape of the yield curve.&#160; This analysis incorporated substantially all
of Bankshares&#146; assets and liabilities and off-balance sheet instruments as of December&nbsp;31,
2005.&#160; Through these simulations,
management estimates the impact on net interest income of a 200 basis point
upward and a 200 basis point downward change in interest rates.&#160; In analyzing interest rate sensitivity for
policy measurement, we compare our forecasted net interest income in both &#147;high
rate&#148; and &#147;low rate&#148; scenarios to our most likely earnings estimate utilizing a
&#147;flat rate&#148; scenario.&#160; The policy
measurement period is 12 months in length, beginning with the first month of
the forecast.&#160; Our objective is to manage
prudently the interest-bearing assets and liabilities on our balance sheet in
ways that minimize our exposure to changes in interest rates.&#160; Our &#147;high rate&#148; and &#147;low rate&#148; scenarios
assume gradual 100 and 200 basis point increases or decreases in the federal
funds rate relative to the &#147;flat rate&#148; scenario.&#160; Our standard approach evaluates expected net
interest income in a 200 basis point range both above and below the &#147;flat rate&#148;
scenario.&#160; However, due to the low
absolute levels of interest rates in 2004, we modified the &#147;low rate&#148; scenario
to measure a decline of 100 basis points.&#160;
To capture the impact of yield curve-related risk, we simultaneously
measure the impact of nonparallel shifts in rates.&#160; A parallel shift would move all points on the
yield curve by the same increments.&#160; A
nonparallel shift would consist of a 100 basis point increase in short-term
rates, while long-term rates would increase by a different amount.&#160; A rate shift in which short-term rates rise
to a greater extent than long-term rates is referred to as a &#147;flattening&#148; of
the yield curve.&#160; Conversely, long-term
rates rising to a greater extent than short-term rates would lead to a &#147;steepening&#148;
of the yield curve.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Federal Reserve Board began tightening monetary policy in June&nbsp;30,
2004.&#160; By December&nbsp;31, 2005, the
Federal Reserve Board had raised interest rates by 325 basis points.&#160; As a result, the historically steep yield
curve environment that persisted in 2004 began to shift to a flatter yield
curve environment.&#160; Accordingly,
throughout 2005 we evaluated rate shifts that included a flattening of the
yield curve.&#160; Interest rate risk
management decisions are made based on a composite view of both parallel and
nonparallel shifts.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

point change and a negative 100 and 200 basis point change in interest rates
would have on Bankshares&#146; net interest income over the next 12 months.</font></p>

  <p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">%</font></p>
  </td>
 </tr>
</table>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">As seen in the &#147;Earnings Sensitivity&#148; table above, within a one-year
horizon, the earnings sensitivity model forecasts that, compared with the net
interest income projection under stable rates, net interest income would
increase by 1.3% and 2.3% if interest rates increased by 100 and 200 basis
points, respectively.&#160; Inversely, if
interest rates decreased by 100 and 200 basis points, net interest income would
decrease by 1.8% and 4.6%, respectively.&#160;
Bankshares manages the interest rate risk profile within policy limits
of +/- 5.0% change in net interest income on a +/- 200 basis point change in
interest rates and at December&nbsp;31, 2005 was within the risk limits
established.&#160; These results are not
necessarily indicative of future actual results, nor do they take into account
certain actions that management may undertake in response to future changes in
interest rates.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Bankshares&#146; Consolidated Balance Sheet had been positioned for a rate
rise, and the increase in 2005 in net interest income reflects some of the
benefit of the Federal Reserve Board rate increases.&#160; In response to action by the Federal Reserve
Board, Bankshares prime interest rate continued to rise. Bankshares has
approximately $4.7 billion in loans that will reprice within the next quarter.
Additionally, in 2005 we continued our investment strategy of shifting the
portfolio mix into a higher percentage of mortgage-backed securities.&#160; We use mortgage-backed securities as a hedge
against both rising and falling interest rates, depending on their purchase
price, which has a significant impact on their yield in different rate
environments.&#160; We selectively include
current coupon mortgage securities in our portfolio as a hedge against a
continued low rate environment.&#160; Mortgage
securities purchased at a discount are used to hedge against declining
rates.&#160; The effects of a rising rate
environment on interest expense are less predictable due to customer behavior
and intense price competition that may shift the mix of deposit products.&#160; Approximately $1.6 billion in short and
long-term debt will also be subject to rate increases in the near term.&#160; Given the current rate environment, the shape
of the yield curve and the competitive dynamic, we anticipate the net interest
margin will be under greater pressure in 2006.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">45</font></p>

<div>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">MARKET VALUE OF EQUITY MODELING</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Bankshares also
utilizes the market value of equity as a measurement tool in managing interest
rate sensitivity.&#160; The market value of
equity measures the degree to which the market values of Bankshares&#146; assets and
liabilities and off-balance sheet instruments will change given a change in
interest rates.&#160; ALCO guidelines limit
the change in market value of equity in a 200 basis point parallel rate shock
to 25% of the market value of equity assuming interest rates at December&nbsp;31,
2005.&#160; The up 200 basis point scenario
resulted in a 2.9% decrease at December&nbsp;31, 2005 and a 2.2% increase at December&nbsp;31,
2004.&#160; The down 200 basis point scenario
resulted in a 3.9% decrease at December&nbsp;31, 2005 and an 8.6% decrease at December&nbsp;31,
2004.&#160; At December&nbsp;31, 2005 and
2004, Bankshares was within its policy guidelines.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The valuation
analysis is dependent upon certain key assumptions about the nature of
indeterminate maturities of assets and liabilities. Management estimates the
average life and rate characteristics of asset and liability accounts based on
historical analysis and management&#146;s expectation of rate behavior.&#160; These assumptions are periodically validated
and updated.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<h5 style="font-weight:bold;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;page-break-after:auto;text-autospace:none;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Market Risk</font></b></h5>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Market risk is defined as the constraint imposed by lower market values
of assets and liabilities as interest rates and equity markets fluctuate.&#160; Changes in market values also affect the fee
income earned by IWM, where a significant portion of the fee schedule&nbsp;is
tied to current asset values under management or administration.&#160; Bankshares has designated substantially all
of its investment portfolio as available-for-sale, and in accordance with
financial reporting standards, this portfolio is reported at fair value.&#160; Changes in fair value, net of tax, are
reflected as a component of shareholders&#146; equity.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Trading Activities</font></i></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Bankshares provides capital market products to its customers.&#160; From a market risk perspective, Bankshares&#146;
net income is exposed to changes in interest rates, credit spreads, and
equities and their implied volatilities.&#160;
The primary purpose of Bankshares&#146; trading business is to accommodate
customers in the management of their market price risks.&#160; Derivative transactions executed with
customers are simultaneously hedged in the capital markets.&#160; All derivatives transacted with customers
used to hedge capital market transactions with customers are carried at fair
value.&#160; The ALCO establishes and monitors
counterparty risk limits.&#160; The notional
amount, exposure amount and estimated net fair value of all customer
accommodation derivatives at December&nbsp;31, 2005 are included in Note No.&nbsp;18
(Derivative Instruments and Hedging Activities) to the financial statements.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Equity Markets</font></i></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Bankshares is
directly and indirectly affected by changes in the equity markets.&#160; Bankshares has made investments in private
equities and hedge funds.&#160; These private
equity investments are made within capital allocations approved by Bankshares&#146;
management. Management reviews these investments at least quarterly and
assesses them for possible other-than-temporary impairment.&#160; For nonmarketable investments, the analysis
is based on the facts and circumstances of each individual investment and the
expectations for that investment&#146;s cash flows and capital needs, the viability
of the business model and an appropriate exit strategy.&#160; Private equity investments totaled $20.7
million at December&nbsp;31, 2005 and $24.7 million at December&nbsp;31,
2004.&#160; Hedge funds investment totaled
$62.8 million at December&nbsp;31, 2005 and $77.5 million at December&nbsp;31,
2004.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Changes in equity
market prices may also indirectly affect Bankshares&#146; net income (1)&nbsp;by
affecting the value of third-party assets under management or administration
within IWM and, hence, fee income; (2)&nbsp;by affecting particular borrowers,
whose ability to repay principal and/or interest may be affected by the stock
market; or (3)&nbsp;by affecting brokerage activity, related commission income
and other business activities.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Bankshares&#146;
maintenance of capital ratios well above regulatory requirements (see &#147;Capital
Resources and Adequacy&#148;) provides management with the flexibility to utilize
the available-for-sale portfolio for liquidity and interest rate risk
management needs, even during a period when valuations are depressed.&#160; Maintaining a fairly short duration in the
portfolio also mitigates market risk.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Liquidity Risk</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Liquidity risk is the possibility that Bankshares will not be able to
fund present and future financial obligations.&#160;
The objective of liquidity management is to maintain the ability to meet
commitments to fund loans, purchase securities and repay deposits and other
liabilities in accordance with their terms.&#160;
To achieve this objective, the ALCO establishes and monitors liquidity
guidelines that require sufficient asset-based liquidity to cover potential
funding requirements and to avoid over-reliance on volatile, less reliable
funding markets.&#160; Debt securities in the
available-for-sale portfolio provide liquidity, in addition to the immediately
liquid resources of cash and due from banks and federal funds sold and
securities purchased under resale agreements.&#160;
By limiting the maturity of securities and maintaining a conservative
investment posture, management can rely on the investment portfolio to help
meet any short-term funding needs. U.S. Treasury and agency securities, which
provide the greatest liquidity, averaged $1.4 billion in 2005, an 8.6% decrease
from the average of $1.6 billion in 2004.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">46</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Core customer deposits historically have provided a substantial source
of relatively stable, low-cost funds.&#160;
During 2005, core deposits (total deposits less certificates of deposit
of $100,000 and over), averaged $9.8 billion compared with $9.1 billion during
2004.&#160; Although not viewed as core
deposits, a substantial portion of short-term borrowings comprised of
securities sold under agreements to repurchase and commercial paper originate
from core deposit relationships tied to the overnight cash management program
offered to customers.&#160; Short-term
borrowings averaged $1.1 billion during 2005, an 18.1% increase from the 2004
level.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In addition to these sources, Bankshares has access to national markets
for certificates of deposit, commercial paper and debt financing.&#160; Should Bankshares need to supplement its
liquidity, it also has $2.1 billion in lines with the Federal Home Loan Bank of
Atlanta (&#147;FHLB&#148;) and back-up commercial paper lines of $40.0 million with
commercial banks.&#160; Bankshares is required
to obtain approval from holders of Bankshares&#146; 6.72% and 6.80% unsecured senior
notes if Bankshares incrementally borrows in excess of $150.0 million under the
FHLB lines.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Long-term debt increased to $742.2 million at December&nbsp;31, 2005
from $690.1 million at December&nbsp;31, 2004, primarily due to the $116.2
million of additional FHLB advances and subordinated debt assumed in the CBNV
acquisition.&#160; During 2005, $118.5 million
was repaid on long-term debt.&#160; Bankshares
can access the capital markets for long-term funding by issuing registered debt
and private placements.&#160; In September&nbsp;2005,
Moody&#146;s Investors Service affirmed Mercantile Bankshares Corporation&#146;s
commercial paper rating of &#147;P-1&#148; and Bankshares&#146; subordinated debt rating of &#147;A2.&#148;&#160; Also in September&nbsp;2005, Standard&nbsp;&amp;
Poor&#146;s Ratings Service affirmed Bankshares&#146; rating of &#147;A+/Stable/A-1&#148; and
counterparty rating of &#147;A+/Stable/A-1.&#148;&#160;
Rating agencies base their ratings on many quantitative and qualitative
factors, including capital adequacy, liquidity, asset quality, quality of the
management team, business mix and the level and quality of earnings.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Capital Resources and Adequacy</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Bankshares has consistently maintained a capital to asset ratio higher
than its peers, as reported in data furnished by its regulators. Shareholders&#146;
equity averaged $2.1 billion during 2005, which represented an increase of
$224.7 million, or 12.0%, over the prior year&#146;s average.&#160; This increase reflected the shares issued in
the CBNV acquisition that were valued at $124.3 million.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Maintenance of capital strength has long been a guiding principle of
Bankshares.&#160; Ample capital is necessary
to sustain growth, to provide a measure of protection against unanticipated
declines in asset values and to safeguard the funds of depositors.&#160; Capital also provides a source of funds to
meet loan demand and enables Bankshares to manage its assets and liabilities
effectively.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Shareholders&#146; equity increased 14.4% to $2.2 billion at year-end 2005
from $1.9 billion at year-end 2004. The increase was attributable primarily to
earnings growth and the CBNV acquisition offset by increased cash dividend
payments.&#160; Book value per share was $17.81
at December&nbsp;31, 2005 compared with $16.12 at December&nbsp;31, 2004.&#160; The ratio of average equity to average assets
was 13.51% in 2005 and 13.38% in 2004, ranking Bankshares among the most
strongly capitalized banks in the industry.&#160;
Excluding intangible assets, average tangible equity to average tangible
assets was 9.70% in both 2005 and 2004.&#160;
Bankshares believes that excluding intangible assets helps the investor
understand the effects of acquisition activities on its results and more
closely approximates the basis for measuring the adequacy of capital for
regulatory purposes.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">While maintaining exceptional capital strength and financing the growth
of the corporation, Bankshares also has pursued a share repurchase
program.&#160; In 2001, the Board of Directors
authorized the repurchase of shares of common stock under these programs.&#160; At December&nbsp;31, 2005, there remained 476,327
shares of common stock authorized for repurchase.&#160; The share repurchase program has supported
management&#146;s strategy to enhance shareholder value.&#160; Management has repurchased shares in open
market and privately negotiated transactions during periods when capital
accumulates at a rate in excess of that required to support the growth of
earning assets.&#160; See Note No.&nbsp;11
(Shareholders&#146; Equity) of the financial statements and the &#147;Statements of
Changes in Consolidated Shareholders&#146; Equity&#148; found elsewhere in this document
for details related to the share repurchase program.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Various bank regulatory agencies have implemented capital guidelines,
which are directly related to a bank&#146;s risk-based capital ratios. By regulatory
definition, a well capitalized institution, such as Bankshares, faces fewer
regulatory constraints on its operations than institutions classified as
undercapitalized.&#160; For example, only well
capitalized banks can accept brokered deposits without advance regulatory approval.&#160; In addition, FDIC deposit insurance premium
rates are significantly lower for banks with higher capital levels. The &#147;Tier I
Capital Ratio&#148; graph above shows that Bankshares has maintained capital levels
well in excess of the regulatory minimum over each of the last five years.&#160; For a further discussion of the regulatory
capital requirements that apply to Bankshares, see Note No.&nbsp;11
(Shareholders&#146; Equity) of the financial statements.&#160; Bank regulatory agencies also impose certain
restrictions on transactions among and between subsidiaries of bank holding
companies, including extensions of credit, transfers of assets and payments of
dividends.&#160; Historically, the dividend
restrictions have not limited dividend payments at Bankshares and it is not
anticipated that they will have a constraining effect in the future.&#160; In addition to dividend restrictions, capital
requirements also are affected by off-balance sheet risks.&#160; These include such items as letters of credit
and commitments to extend credit. Refer to Note No.&nbsp;10 (Commitments and
Contingencies) of the financial statements for information regarding Bankshares&#146;
commitments.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">DIVIDENDS</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Bankshares has paid quarterly cash dividends on its common stock since September&nbsp;1970
when such stock was first issued. Bankshares intends to consider quarterly
payment of dividends on its common stock, but such payment is necessarily
dependent on many factors, including the future earnings and financial
requirements of Bankshares and its affiliates.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On January&nbsp;10, 2006, Bankshares&#146; Board of Directors announced a
three-for-two stock split on its common stock. In addition, the Board stated
its intention to raise the indicated quarterly per share dividend rate,
adjusted for the stock split, to $0.26 per share.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">For the 29th consecutive year, the annual dividend paid on common stock
exceeded the prior year&#146;s level.&#160; Effective
with the June&nbsp;2005 dividend, the quarterly cash dividend, adjusted for the
stock split, was increased 8.7% to $0.25 from $0.23 per share.&#160; Over the last five years, dividends have
increased at a compound growth rate of 7.8 %.&#160;
Management periodically will evaluate the dividend rate in light of
Bankshares&#146; capital strength, profitability and conditions prevailing in the
economy in general and the banking industry in particular.&#160; The annual dividends paid per common share
were $0.99 in 2005 and $0.92 in 2004.&#160;
Total cash dividends paid were $120.2 million in 2005 and $109.3 million
in 2004.&#160; The &#147;Dividends&#148; table above
presents quarterly dividends paid over the last two years.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Off-Balance Sheet Arrangements and
Contractual Obligations</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Off-Balance Sheet Arrangements</font></i></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Bankshares consolidates majority-owned subsidiaries that it
controls.&#160; Other affiliates, including
certain joint ventures in which there is less than 20% ownership, generally are
carried at the lower of cost or fair market value.&#160; Bankshares does not dispose of troubled loans
or problem assets by means of unconsolidated special purpose entities.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">One of Bankshares&#146; mortgage banking subsidiaries, as a Fannie Mae
Delegated Underwriting and Servicing lender, has a loss sharing arrangement for
loans originated on behalf of and sold to Fannie Mae.&#160; In the ordinary course of business,
Bankshares routinely originates and sells mortgage loans on the secondary
market.&#160; Typically, these loans are sold
under forward commitments.&#160; Refer to Note
No.&nbsp;10 (Commitments and Contingencies) of the financial statements for
additional information regarding commitments relating to mortgage banking.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<div>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Contractual Obligations and Other Commitments</font></i></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Through the normal course of business, Bankshares enters into certain
contractual obligations and other commitments.&#160;
Such obligations generally relate to funding operations through debt
arrangements as well as leases of premises and equipment.&#160; It is estimated that approximately $36.0 million
of capital expenditures for new and existing banking offices and replacement of
furniture, equipment and technology will occur in 2006.&#160; While these items have been included in the
budget for 2006, they are subject to a review and approval process prior to
funding.&#160; For further information on
commitments, see Notes No.&nbsp;5, 9 and 10 of the financial statements.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">As a financial services provider, Bankshares routinely enters into
commitments to extend credit, including loan commitments, standby letters of credit
and financial guarantees.&#160; Guarantees are
contracts that contingently require us to make payments to a guaranteed party
based on an event or changes in an underlying asset, liability, rate or index.&#160; While contractual obligations represent
future cash requirements of Bankshares, a significant portion of commitments to
extend credit are likely to expire without being drawn upon.&#160; Such commitments are subject to the same
credit policies and approval processes accorded to loans made by Bankshares.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Additionally, Bankshares has committed to invest funds in third-party
private equity investments.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The table below summarizes significant contractual obligations and
other commitments:</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<table border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" width="100%" style="border-collapse:collapse;width:100.0%;">
 <tr>
  <td width="36%" valign="bottom" style="padding:0in 0in 0in 0in;width:36.12%;">
  <p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><b><font size="1" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:1.0pt;font-weight:bold;">&nbsp;</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">REVIEW OF EARNINGS AND
BALANCE SHEET FOR 2004 TO 2003</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Performance&nbsp;&amp; Operating
Analysis</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In the third quarter of
2004, Bankshares consolidated 11 affiliate banks into four banks.&#160; The consolidated banks shared common
markets.&#160; The consolidation of these banks
enables the surviving banks to serve their local customers with greater size,
scale and expertise.&#160; This initiative was
not undertaken to reduce operating costs, although some savings arose out of
the consolidation.&#160; It was to enable
these banks to streamline operating processes, controls and compliance efforts;
recruit seasoned professionals to these markets; and provide a greater breadth
of services at the local level.&#160;
Bankshares is committed to the affiliate bank model, whereby local
boards of directors provide strong oversight, and bank presidents maintain
strong relationships within the community. As with any strategic initiative,
costs are involved.&#160; In 2004, Banking
incurred approximately $3.6 million in restructuring charges related to the
consolidations.&#160; A majority of these
costs were in severance charges and other personnel costs of approximately $2.3
million with $1.1 million in legal and consulting fees.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Net income in 2004 was
$229.4 million compared with $196.8 million in 2003, a 16.6% increase.&#160; Diluted net income per common share was $1.92
in 2004 compared with $1.79 in 2003, an increase of 7.3%.&#160; Return on average assets was 1.64%, and
return on average equity was 12.26% in 2004 compared with 1.64% and 13.15%,
respectively, in 2003.&#160; The decrease in
return on average equity was due primarily to equity issued in the Farmers acquisition.&#160; Average assets increased 16.9% to $14.0
billion; average deposits increased 15.8% to $10.4 billion; and average loans
increased 20.2% to $9.7 billion for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2004
compared with the prior year.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Net interest income, on a
fully tax-equivalent basis, was $552.5 million in 2004 compared with $479.1
million in 2003.&#160; Both changes in the
level of interest rates and changes in the amount and composition of
interest-earning assets and interest-bearing liabilities affected net interest
income.&#160; In response to the improving
economy, the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (&#147;Federal Reserve
Board&#148;) began increasing short-term interest rates.&#160; After reducing short-term rates by 50 basis
points in 2002 and 25 basis points in 2003, the Federal Reserve Board increased
short-term rates 125 basis points in 2004.&#160;
By year-end 2004, the benchmark targeted overnight federal funds rate
had risen from 1.00% to 2.25%.&#160; Although
the net interest margin improved only 3&nbsp;basis points to 4.35% for 2004
from 4.32% for 2003, this compared very favorably with the 33 basis point
decline experienced during 2003.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Noninterest income for
2004 increased by $30.4 million, or 16.5%, to $213.9 million compared with
$183.6 million for 2003. The increases over 2003 were significantly affected in
nearly every category by the inclusion of Farmers for a full year, which was
acquired on August&nbsp;12, 2003.&#160;
Stronger equity markets on average during 2004 fueled the $90.1 million,
or 14.1%, increase in IWM revenues over 2003.&#160;
Additionally, the investment in nonmarketable investments (private
equity, hedge funds and other investments) improved with the stronger equity
markets.&#160; Income from private equity and
other investments increased $1.7 million, or 212.2%, in 2004, offset slightly
by a decline in income from hedge funds of $0.9 million, or 13.4%, in 2004.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Noninterest expenses
increased $54.5 million, or 16.2%, from 2003.&#160;
The principal reasons for the year-over-year increase were the full-year
inclusion of Farmers, Boyd Watterson and Peremel; costs related to the
consolidation of 11 bank affiliates into four; costs related to conversion and
outsourcing the IWM back-office to SunGard; and increased professional services
related to compliance costs.&#160; Salaries
increased $27.3 million, or 17.0%.&#160;
Nearly one-third of this increase ($9.2 million) was due to Farmers,
Boyd Watterson and Peremel included in 2004 for a full year.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Net occupancy expense
increased by $3.6 million, or 17.1%, during 2004 due to inclusion for a full
year of 39 net additional branch locations as well as three corporate offices
related to acquisitions.&#160; Mitigating a
portion of this expense was $1.2 million related to the termination of certain
Banking lease agreements, due primarily to the Farmers integration concluded in
2004.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Professional fees
increased $5.8 million in 2004.&#160; Professional
services increased with costs incurred in connection with the investigation of
potential acquisitions of $1.0 million, legal costs related to investigatory
and litigation matters that, in management&#146;s view, were not normal recurring
expenses of $2.5 million, and compliance implementation costs of $2.5 million
related to Section&nbsp;404 of The Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">50</font></p>

<div>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Segment Reporting</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In the fourth quarter of
2005, the Private Banking Group of MSD&amp;T was consolidated into the Private Banking
Group of IWM. The segment results have been reclassified to conform to current
presentation for comparability.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Banking</font></i></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Net income in 2004 was $220.9
million compared with $192.5 million in 2003, a 14.7% increase.&#160; For the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2004,
average assets increased 15.8% to $13.4 billion; average deposits increased 14.6%
to $10.3 billion; and average loans increased 20.4% to $9.6 billion.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Net interest income, on a
fully tax-equivalent basis, was $539.0 million in 2004 compared with $474.6
million in 2003.&#160; The increase in net
interest income was attributable to a 14.7% increase in average earning assets,
which more than offset a decline of 4 basis points in the net interest margin.
Contributing to the net interest margin decline was the capital restructuring
of the banks during the third quarter of 2003.&#160;
Subordinated debt totaling $300 million, issued by Bankshares in April&nbsp;2003,
and used in part to fund the cash portion of the Farmers acquisition, was
invested in a like amount of subordinated debt issued by the banks. &#160;Excess equity capital was paid to Bankshares
in the form of a special cash dividend.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The year-over-year
increases in noninterest income and noninterest expenses from 2003 were attributable
primarily to the inclusion of Farmers for a full year and the branch expansion
programs.&#160; Noninterest income increased
to $114.5 million in 2004 from $98.4 million in 2003 with deposit service
charges increasing by $5.1 million, insurance fees increasing by $8.7 million
and electronic banking fees increasing by $4.8 million, accounting for the
largest gains.&#160; These gains were
partially offset by a decrease of $6.8 million in net gains on investment
securities sold.&#160; Noninterest expenses
increased to $318.7 million in 2004 from $268.7 million in 2003.&#160; More than 72% of this increase was related to
salaries and benefits, which grew by $32.7 million.&#160; Severance costs related to the affiliate bank
consolidations were approximately $2.3 million.&#160;
Occupancy expense increased by $3.1 million, and amortization of
intangible assets increased by $2.6 million, while furniture and equipment
expenses decreased by $1.3 million.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">IWM</font></i></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On November&nbsp;12,
2004, Bankshares consolidated its brokerage activities by merging Mercantile
Securities,&nbsp;Inc. into Peremel. The resulting entity, Mercantile Brokerage
Services,&nbsp;Inc., is a general securities broker-dealer that offers
full-service, discount and online brokerage services.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Net income in 2004 was
$16.5 million compared with $11.4 million in 2003.&#160; Pretax profit margins, prior to corporate
overhead allocations, were 31.1% and 26.3% for 2004 and 2003,
respectively.&#160; At December&nbsp;31, 2004,
assets under administration by IWM were $47.8 billion, an increase of $1.8
billion from the prior year.&#160; Bankshares
had investment management responsibility for $21.1&nbsp;billion at December&nbsp;31,
2004 and 2003.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Revenues increased $14.3
million, or 16.5%, to $100.7 million in 2004 from $86.4 million in 2003.&#160; Revenue increases were achieved in the three
principal client segments:&#160; private
wealth, institutional and brokerage.&#160;
Growth in IWM revenues was due principally to stronger markets during
2004 than 2003, new business development efforts and the inclusion of a full
year&#146;s results for Boyd Watterson and Peremel, which were acquired on March&nbsp;1,
2003 and April&nbsp;1, 2003, respectively.&#160;
Together, these acquisitions accounted for $2.4 million of the increase
in revenues.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Expenses increased 8.9%
to $69.6 million in 2004.&#160; Increases in
legal and professional service expenses were offset largely by decreases in
personnel-related and technology expenses.&#160;
Also contributing to the increase was the inclusion of a full year&#146;s
results for Boyd Watterson and Peremel.&#160;
Expenses for 2003 included $3.6 million of severance and $0.5 million
paid to terminate a technology equipment lease.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">During the first quarter
of 2004, Bankshares entered into a seven-year service contract with SunGard
Wealth Management Services (&#147;SunGard&#148;) to provide a new core accounting system
and back-office operations beginning in January&nbsp;2005.&#160; In 2004, IWM incurred approximately $0.9
million in restructuring charges related to the conversion to SunGard&#146;s
AddVantage trust accounting system.&#160; A
majority of these costs were severance charges of approximately $0.6
million.&#160; Conversion costs of
approximately $1.8 million that were incurred in 2004 are being amortized over
the life of the contract.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Credit Quality Measures</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Provision for loan losses
was $7.2 million in 2004 compared with $12.1 million in 2003.&#160; Net charge-offs in 2004 were $13.6 million,
or 0.14% of average total loans compared with $8.6 million, or 0.11%, in
2003.&#160; The allowance for loan losses was
$149.0 million, or 1.46% of total loans, at December&nbsp;31, 2004 compared
with $155.3 million, or 1.68%, at December&nbsp;31, 2003.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">At December&nbsp;31,
2004, total nonperforming assets were $31.1 million, or 0.30% of total loans,
compared with $50.4 million, or 0.55%, at December&nbsp;31, 2003.&#160; The decline primarily relates to acceptance
of payment and charge-off of a nonperforming loan in the fourth quarter of
2004.&#160; The restoration of one customer to
full accrual status accounted for $2.5 million of the $5.4 million decrease in
commercial real estate nonaccrual loans.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">51</font></p>

<div>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Capital Ratios</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The ratio of average
shareholders&#146; equity to average total assets was 13.38% for 2004 and 12.51% for
2003.&#160; Bankshares&#146; total risk-based
capital ratio at December&nbsp;31, 2004 was 16.23%, and Tier I capital ratio
was 12.33%, exceeding the minimum regulatory guidelines of 8.0% and 4.0%,
respectively.&#160; Bankshares&#146; leverage
ratios were 10.02% and 9.60% at December&nbsp;31, 2004 and 2003, respectively,
exceeding the minimum regulatory guideline of 4.0%.&#160; As of December&nbsp;31, 2004, all of
Bankshares&#146; bank affiliates exceeded all capital adequacy requirements necessary
to be considered &#147;well capitalized.&#148;&#160; For
additional information on Bankshares&#146; risk-based capital ratios, see Note No.&nbsp;11
(Shareholders&#146; Equity) of the financial statements.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">QUARTERLY RESULTS OF
OPERATIONS</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The following is a
summary of the quarterly results of operations.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">RECONCILIATION OF NON-GAAP
MEASURES</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">We believe the non-GAAP
measures we use provide information useful to investors in understanding our
ongoing core business and operational performance trends.&#160; These measures should not be viewed as a
substitute for GAAP.&#160; Management believes
presentations of financial measures excluding the impact of certain items
provide useful supplemental information and better reflect its core operating
activities.&#160; In order to arrive at core
business operations results, the effects of certain non-core business
transactions such as gains and losses on the sales of securities, amortization
of intangibles, restructuring charges and merger-related expenses, have been
excluded.&#160; Management reviews these same
measures internally.&#160; For instance, the
cash operating efficiency ratio, rather than the GAAP basis efficiency ratio,
is used to measure management&#146;s success at controlling ongoing, core operating
expenses.&#160; Additionally, management
believes that reporting several key measures based on tangible assets (total
assets less intangible assets) and tangible equity (total equity less intangible
assets) is important as this more closely approximates the basis for measuring
the adequacy of capital for regulatory purposes.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

  <p align="right" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:right;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">145,370</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">(2)&nbsp;Management
excludes the balance of intangible assets and their related amortization
expense from its calculation of return on</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">average tangible equity
and average tangible equity to average tangible assets.&#160; This adjustment allows management to review
the</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">core operating results
and core capital position of Bankshares.&#160;
This is consistent with the treatment by the bank regulatory agencies</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">that excludes goodwill
and other intangible assets from their calculation of risk-based capital
ratios.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">(3)&nbsp;The efficiency
ratio is measured by dividing noninterest expenses by the sum of net interest
income on an FTE basis and</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">noninterest income.&#160; When computing the cash operating efficiency
ratio and cash operating earnings, management excludes the amortization of
intangible assets, restructuring charges, merger-related expenses, and gains
and losses on sales of premises and from sales of investment securities in
order to assess the core operating results of Bankshares and because of the
uncertainty as to timing and amount of gain or loss to be recognized.</font></p>
